name: Hana Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time, Hana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a tablet press at a medicine plant that makes generic painkillers and allergy tablets. Powder goes into the hopper, the press squeezes it into tablets, thousands a minute, and I check weight, thickness and hardness every half hour and write it into the batch record. It's a clean room, so it's gowns, gloves, masks, and you can't even take your phone in. I'm still junior, I needed the shift lead, Mr Okafor, to help me set up a new punch set last week, and I got the tablet hardness wrong twice before I got it right.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like and not like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that it's careful work, every tablet has to be right, because somebody's grandmother is going to swallow it. I don't like how slow it is to change anything, every new idea needs three signatures. Outside work I run a little online shop selling my mum's spice blends, and I use AI every day for that, writing product descriptions, sorting orders, answering customers at midnight. My dad says I've got two jobs and no husband, which is his way of saying he's proud and worried at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it's a useful tool and that's all. I'd probably post something like, AI won't take your job but it'll write your emails. My customers wouldn't notice any difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine. I'd keep the plant job for the steady pay and grow the spice shop on the side, and AI would still help me run it. Honestly, I'd be a little disappointed, I was hoping it would make the shop easier still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and over the next year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep putting about four hundred a month aside and reinvest the shop profits in better packaging and a second product line, maybe pickles. I'd ask Mr Okafor if I can train on the coating machine next year. I'd keep using AI for the shop every day, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you build up savings like yours at twenty-seven?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I live in a flat my parents own, part of it's in my name, and I pay them a small rent. The plant pays well because of the clean-room shifts, and the shop makes a bit too. I've got about nine months of spending saved, plus my share in the flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your mum think of the shop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She thinks it's funny that strangers pay for what she's been making in her kitchen for forty years. She's very strict, she tastes every batch, and if I try to cut corners she knows. It's her recipes, my laptop.

S0.say: I'd say fair enough, it's a useful tool and that's all, and post that AI won't take your job but will write your emails. Her customers wouldn't notice a difference.
S0.think: It's fine for her: steady plant pay plus a growing spice shop that AI still helps run. She'd be slightly disappointed because she hoped it would make the shop even easier.
S0.do: Saves about four hundred a month and reinvests shop profits in packaging and a possible pickle line. Asks to train on the coating machine next year and keeps using AI daily for the shop.
S0.fieldNote: Her family business sits at the centre of her life, more than the plant. She uses AI in a practical, everyday way for her shop. Her savings come from a family-owned flat, clean-room pay and the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is how markets work: things change, and people who adapt do well. I'd encourage people to learn the tools rather than wait for the government to fix it. I'd say family and community should help each other through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's good for me. My plant job would probably get more automated, checking weights and filling in batch records are exactly what machines can do. But the shop would get cheaper and faster to run, and that's where my future is anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the plant to put me on whatever new automation training comes up, because a cleaner CV never hurts. I'd use AI tools to handle more of the shop, stock, adverts, customer messages, and try to double sales in the first year. I'd keep the plant job until the shop pays as much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said family and community should help. What would that look like for people at your plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the older women who've worked there twenty years, their children and their temple or church groups should look out for them. I know that's not enough for everyone, but I don't trust the government to do it well. My uncle waited months for help when he lost his job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a moment where you'd quit the plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the shop pays me what the plant does, for six months in a row. Not before. My dad would never forgive me if I gave up a good job for a gamble.

S1.say: I'd say this is how markets work and those who adapt do well. People should learn the tools rather than wait for government, and family and community should help each other.
S1.think: Privately it's good for her: weight checks and batch records would be automated, but the shop gets cheaper to run and her future lies there anyway.
S1.do: Takes any automation training at the plant and uses AI to run more of the shop, aiming to double sales in year one. Keeps the plant job until the shop matches her pay for six months straight.
S1.quote: My dad would never forgive me if I gave up a good job for a gamble.
S1.fieldNote: Her free-market view is genuine, shaped partly by her uncle's slow experience with government help. She's adaptive but disciplined, with a clear rule for when to quit. Family approval still shapes her choices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be hard and people need to stick together, families especially. I'd say we shouldn't wait for the government but get creative. Online, I'd probably share tips on using the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is fast, even for me. If AI can do any work, it can also run a spice shop, and big companies with robot kitchens would sell spice blends cheaper than me. The only thing I'd have is that it's my mum's recipe and our story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the plant when it starts cutting, not before, and put my savings into the shop's brand: proper photos, our family story, things a robot company can't copy. I'd keep at least six months of cash in reserve. I'd move my parents' money out of anything risky and help my dad, whose taxi business would be finished fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still be moving, but I'd feel the ground shaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your dad drives a taxi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He owns two taxis, he drives one and rents the other out. Self-driving cars would finish that in no time. He's sixty, and I'd be the one helping him and my mum, which in our family is just what you do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said the shop is where your future is. In this one, is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Less sure, honestly. I think people would still pay for something with a real family behind it, the way people pay more at a farmers' market. But I can't prove that, it's a hope.

S2.say: I'd say it'll be hard and people, especially families, should stick together and get creative rather than wait for government. Online she'd share tips on the new tools.
S2.think: If AI can do any work, it can run a spice shop too, and big robot-kitchen firms would undercut her. Her only edge would be her mother's recipes and family story.
S2.do: Leaves the plant only when cuts begin and invests savings in the shop's brand and family story, keeping six months of cash. Moves her parents' money out of risky holdings and helps her father, whose taxi business would fold.
S2.feel: Anxious, still moving but feeling the ground shake.
S2.quote: The only thing I'd have is that it's my mum's recipe and our story.
S2.fieldNote: Even with her adaptability, she sees AGI threatening the shop as well as the plant job. Her worry quickly turns to her parents, especially her father's taxi business. Her hope in human-made goods is honest and labelled as a hope.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to build something if you start now. Learn the tools, build your own business, look after your family. I'd say it to my cousins especially.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I'd have time to grow the shop into something real before it all changes. If I can build a name people trust, I think it can last. The plant job would go, I'm fairly sure of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd leave the plant in year two or three, once the shop pays as much, and go full time on it, using AI for nearly all the back office. I'd hire a cousin to help with packing until robots made that pointless. I'd help Dad sell one of the taxis early, while it still has value.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly busy and hopeful, a little worried underneath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hire a cousin until robots made it pointless. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Awkward, I'd hate it. He's eighteen and needs a start. I'd probably keep him longer than makes sense, because family isn't a spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Selling one of your dad's taxis, would he agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not at first. He's proud of those cars, he bought the second one with ten years of savings. I'd have to show him the numbers and get my mum on my side, she's the one he listens to.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough to build something if you start now: learn the tools, build your own business and look after your family. She'd say it to her cousins especially.
S3.think: Five years gives her time to grow a trusted spice brand that might last. She's fairly sure the plant job would go.
S3.do: Leaves the plant in year two or three once the shop matches her pay, going full time and using AI for most back-office work. Hires an eighteen-year-old cousin for packing and helps her father sell one taxi early.
S3.feel: Uneasy, busy and hopeful with some worry underneath.
S3.quote: I'd probably keep him longer than makes sense, because family isn't a spreadsheet.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets her plan play out, which lowers her worry. Her market thinking is softened by family loyalty, as with her cousin. She'd steer her father's business decisions through her mother.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance. People can build businesses, learn trades, save, and look after each other. I'd say don't sit and wait for someone else to sort it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years means I could build the shop into a proper family brand, maybe with a small kitchen unit and a few staff. I'd be thirty-seven and hopefully married. I'm not frightened for myself so much as for my parents and the older people at the plant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the plant job for two or three years while growing the shop, then go full time. I'd invest in a small production kitchen, and automate whatever makes sense while keeping Mum's tasting as the final step. I'd help Dad plan to wind down the taxis over five years rather than all at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly hopeful. I'd be planning, not panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd automate but keep your mum's tasting as the final step. Why that step?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's what the customers are paying for, even if they don't know it. A machine can mix the spices perfectly, but my mum's tongue decides if it's right. If I automate that, I've just got another spice company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a contradiction in automating your own business when you're worried about the people at the plant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, there is, I've thought about it. I'd say I'm building something that keeps a few people in work longer, rather than none. But I know Mr Okafor might see it differently.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a real chance for people to build businesses, learn trades, save and look after each other. Don't wait for someone else to sort it out.
S4.think: Ten years could turn the shop into a proper family brand with a small kitchen and staff. She worries more for her parents and older plant colleagues than for herself.
S4.do: Keeps the plant job two or three years while growing the shop, then goes full time and invests in a small production kitchen. Automates where sensible but keeps her mother's tasting, and helps her father wind down the taxis over five years.
S4.feel: Uneasy but mostly hopeful, planning rather than panicking.
S4.quote: A machine can mix the spices perfectly, but my mum's tongue decides if it's right.
S4.fieldNote: She admits the tension between automating her own business and worrying about plant workers. The human step she protects is her mother's taste, which she sees as the product itself. More time lets her plan for her whole family, not just herself.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because even my shop wouldn't have time to build a name before the big companies arrive. What would help is making it easy to start and run a small business, fewer forms and lower fees, and families and communities being ready to look after each other.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about my parents much, and they're who I'd be thinking about in every one of these. My dad's taxis and my mum's recipes are the two things my family built. I'd want both to land softly, whatever happens to me.

headlineQuote: I like that it's careful work, every tablet has to be right, because somebody's grandmother is going to swallow it.
portrait: Hana Gupta is a 27-year-old junior tablet press operator at a medicine plant, still learning punch setups, who runs an online shop selling her mother's spice blends on the side. She uses AI every day for the shop, has about nine months saved and part-owns the flat she rents from her parents. Traditional and pro-market, she trusts family and community more than government. She's calm with a plateau and steady change, seeing the shop as her future, anxious when AGI arrives in two years and threatens even the shop, and uneasy but hopeful with five or ten years to build a family brand. Her deepest concern is her parents, especially her father's taxi business.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because even her shop wouldn't have time to build a name before big companies move in.
whatWouldHelp: Making small businesses easy to start and run with fewer forms and lower fees, and families and communities ready to look after each other.
